title: Even amid equivocation, a real split remains vs. those who allow only conjectural certainty
source_text: XLVI. Quaecunque autem aequivocatio lateat in ista voce certitudo fidei, quae in Schola Rom. strictius, pro sola certitudine quam articulis fidei, sive expresso Dei verbo praebemus: Apud Protestantes vero latius usurpatur, & extenditur ad ea quae non ex solo Dei verbo proxime & immediate, sed ex aliis etiam aliunde notis deducuntur, ac proinde jure merito videri possit certamen solum de vocibus esse, inter Protestantes & eos Scholae Rom. Theologos qui agnoscunt in fidelibus reperiri posse certitudinem tantam de accepta gratia, ut excludat omnem formidinem, licet istam certitudinem non fidei divinae, sed moralem solum dici velint, nihilominus aliquod reale dissidium manet, inter eosdem Protestantes, & Doctores illos Ecclesiae Rom. qui volunt, absque quadam speciali revelatione, locum hic habere posse certitudinem tantum conjecturalem, quae sit jam dicta morali inferior, nec ut illa omnem formidinem deceptionis excludat, a quo vehementer omnes Protestantes abhorrent.
pass_a_gloss: But whatever equivocation may lurk in that word certainty of faith, which in the Roman School is used more strictly for only the certainty which we give to the articles of faith or to the express Word of God: but among Protestants is used more widely and extended to those things which are deduced not from God’s Word alone proximately and immediately, but also from other things known from elsewhere—and therefore with good right the contest can seem to be only about words between Protestants and those theologians of the Roman School who acknowledge that in the faithful there can be found so great certainty concerning received grace that it excludes every fear, although they want that certainty called not of divine faith but only moral—nevertheless some real disagreement remains between the same Protestants and those doctors of the Roman Church who want, without a certain special revelation, only conjectural certainty to be able to have place here, which is inferior to the already-mentioned moral and does not, as that does, exclude every fear of deception—from which all Protestants vehemently shrink.
pass_b_english: Word-fights with moral-certainty Romanists can be largely verbal.
The hard disagreement is with conjectural-only doctors who never shut out fear of deception.
